idiom_name: send wrapper snapshotting into a bounded Channel<T> side queue with an itemDropped counter
implementation_notes: The BCL ships the secondary channel, not the tap: wrap the sender/endpoint so every outbound message is copied and pushed to a bounded System.Threading.Channels Channel<T> before the original proceeds untouched to the primary receiver. Thread model: ChannelWriter.TryWrite is a synchronous, lock-protected enqueue that returns without ever blocking the caller (drop modes return true even when the item is discarded; only a Wait-mode full channel returns false), and the analyzer runs as a separate background task draining reader.ReadAllAsync() on the ThreadPool - with AllowSynchronousContinuations=false (the CreateBounded default) no reader continuation runs on the producer's thread, so the tap is genuinely out-of-band. Copy semantics: Channel<T> carries references, not values, so the wrapper must write an immutable snapshot (a record or explicit Clone) - the guide's own pattern is `coordinates with {...}` - otherwise the analyzer aliases whatever the primary flow still mutates. Overflow policy is explicit via BoundedChannelFullMode: Wait makes WriteAsync asynchronously block the producer (backpressure couples the analyzer's slowness straight into the primary flow - a policy, not a default accident; note CreateBounded(capacity) defaults to Wait), DropOldest keeps the freshest samples, DropNewest keeps the oldest, DropWrite discards the arriving copy. Because all three drop modes report success, the only truthful loss signal is the itemDropped callback of the CreateBounded(options, itemDropped) overload - wire it to a counter/metric. Choose this form for in-process taps: cheap, removable by not wrapping, no dependency beyond the shared framework (System.Threading.Channels since .NET Core 3.0). Alternates: TPL Dataflow BroadcastBlock<T> is a one-slot broadcast buffer - it holds at most one element, overwriting it as new messages arrive, so a lagging consumer silently misses items with no counter - and it clones only if you pass the source-amending cloningFunction; with a null func every linked target gets the SAME instance, which defeats copy independence. When an ActiveMQ broker is already in the stack, the NMS (.NET) client gets a first-class wire tap broker-side: enable the mirroredQueue destination interceptor and the .NET consumer subscribes to the mirror topic (e.g. VirtualTopic.Mirror.Foo.Bar or <queue>.qmirror) without touching producers or primary consumers - Apache's own docs call it 'a zero-configuration Wire Tap'; a compositeQueue with forwardOnly=false does the same for one named queue by copying to a notification topic before enqueueing.
pitfalls: Channel.CreateBounded(capacity) silently defaults to BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait: there WriteAsync asynchronously blocks the producer when the buffer is full, so a stalled analyzer propagates backpressure into the primary flow - and TryWrite under Wait returns false, dropping every tap copy the moment the buffer fills. Set FullMode deliberately.

Under DropWrite/DropOldest/DropNewest a full channel discards the copy yet TryWrite/WriteAsync still report success (the runtime source comment on DropWrite reads 'Just ignore the item being added but say we added it'), so without the CreateBounded(options, itemDropped) callback the tap loses messages invisibly - the itemDropped hook fires on every drop and is the only place to count them.

Channel<T> transports references, not copies: TryWrite(m) hands the analyzer the same live object the primary handler still mutates, so snapshot to an immutable record or Clone before writing - copy independence is the tap author's job, the channel provides none.

Channel.CreateUnbounded never applies backpressure and grows without limit, so a slow analyzer turns the 'best-effort' tap into an unbounded memory leak on the primary path - and setting AllowSynchronousContinuations = true runs reader continuations inline on the writer's thread, making the analyzer's latency part of the sender's call again.

BroadcastBlock<T> exposes at most one element and overwrites it as new messages arrive, and its cloningFunction may be null to mean 'no cloning performed' - without a real clone func every linked target (primary and analyzer) receives the SAME instance, and a consumer that was busy simply missed whatever single message was in the slot, with no drop signal.
sources: Hohpe, Woolf. Enterprise Integration Patterns, Addison-Wesley 2003, ISBN 0-321-20067-5 — Wire Tap pattern (channel chapter).
